Ottawa’s 85 Year Temperature Report

What’s Happening with Ottawa’s Temperature?

Author

John Lewis

Published

June 14, 2026

1 Executive Summary

Analysis of Ottawa’s 85-year temperature record (1940–2024) confirms that the city is undergoing significant and accelerating warming, consistent with — and in fact exceeding — global and Northern Hemisphere trends. Over the full period, Ottawa’s mean annual temperature has risen at a rate of +0.168°C per decade, roughly 27% faster than the global average of +0.133°C/decade, a pattern consistent with amplified warming in continental interiors and higher latitudes. The warming is not uniform across time: a structural change-point analysis identifies a major climate regime shift around 1997, after which the rate of warming quintupled — from a statistically insignificant slope of 0.003°C/year (1940–1997) to a highly significant 0.013°C/year (1997–2024). Winter months are warming fastest, with December’s trend of 0.042°C/year (p < 0.001) being particularly striking, while the 2020s decade average of +1.33°C anomaly stands in sharp contrast to the -0.41°C of the 1940s. Paralleling the mean shift, the character of extreme events has also transformed in that cold temperature anomalies dominated the record through the 1980s, but a crossover occurred in the late 1980s after which heat temperature anomalies have become increasingly dominant — a change that is clearly visible in both the ridge density distributions and the decade-by-decade extreme frequency analysis.

“Segmented Trend / Acceleration”. This plot directly quantifies the central finding of the report: Figure 2 warming is not just occurring, it is accelerating. The contrasting slopes of the two segments (pre- and post-1997) make the quintupling of the warming rate immediately visible.

“Extreme anomaly frequency by decade”. This figure Figure 1 shows that Ottawa’s climate is not just shifting in its average but that the nature of its extreme events has flipped. The crossing of the cold (blue) and warm (red) extreme frequency lines in the late 1980s is an intuitive indicating that the baseline climate has fundamentally changed.

Together, these two graphs tell the essential story that warming has structurally shifted gears around 1997, and the consequence is a redistribution from cold temperature extremes toward heat extremes which is already underway.

2 Introduction

“The world has been heating up for the past 100 years or so. As a result weather patterns are changing” (A really simple guide to climate change: 14 Jan. 2026, BBC.com/news). As evidence, recent climate headlines have stated “The Pace of Climate Change Has Almost Doubled in Ten Years” , “Climate: Which cities saw record heat last year?” or “Have We Crossed a Dangerous Warming Threshold? …”. Further to this many climate scientists have written that global temperatures in 2025 averaged 1.47 degrees above pre-industrial levels which is uncomfortably close to a key benchmark of 1.5 degrees Celsius for global atmosphere temperatures. The earth is warming at a rate of \(0.35 ºC\) per decade, nearly double the rate of \(0.2 ºC\) per decade in the 1970s. (Nature | Vol 651 | 19 March 2026) Copernicus, a European Climate Change Service, has found that last year was the third-warmest year on record, after 2024 and 2023 and along with 2016 as one of the warmest years this century. The trend is clear that the last 11 years have been the 11 hottest since Copernicus started keeping records in 1950. Given these concerns let’s look at how Ottawa fits into the global and northern hemisphere temperature pattern.

3 Data sources

Ottawa annual and monthly temperatures, for a time span of 85 years (1940-2024), were downloaded from the Environment Canada website.

Variable Source Period Resolution
Ottawa Environment Canada (OTTAWA MACDONALD-CARTIER INT’L A) 1940-2024 Daily
Northern Hemisphere HadCRUT5.1 (nh_ann.csv) 1940-2024 Annual
Global HadCRUT5.1 (global.annual.csv) 1940-2024 Annual

Ottawa temperature anomalies are computed as deviations from the 1940-2024 monthly climatological mean for each calendar month. Winter seasons span December,January,February (DJF), with December associated with the following calendar year (e.g., December 1999 belongs to Winter 2000).

4 Ottawa Annual Temperature Overview



This figure portrays the annual temperature for Ottawa from 1940-2024. The mean temperature for the 85 year period is \(6.3 ºC\) The annual temperature starts off in the early forties as cooler with some warming towards the end of that decade then with some cooling occurring through the 1950s and 60s after which a start of an upward warming in the annual mean temperature that continues into the mid 1980s. However, at this point in the temperature series, the warming begin to accelerate upward continuing in this manner to 2024. This description is seen nicely by the 10 year mean average curve on the plot. The other observation of this temperature series is the substantial variability (volatility) from year to year with a given standard deviation of +/- \(11.2 ºC\).

By dealing with deviations (\(x_i - \bar{x}\)) rather than raw values, there is a shift in the focus from the scale of the data to the relationships within it. So all of the following graphs of temperature will be plotted as deviation form the mean or trend (anomalies). Also this is the method used in the recording procedure for the Global and Northern Hemisphere long term temperature data.



This above plot focus on the annual temperatures statistical trends for Ottawa from 1940 to 2024. The two obvious observations are the upward trend in the data during this 85 year period shown in both the linear trend and the local regression non-linear trend (blue line). Notice the dip in the local trend line indicating a cooler period from the early 1950s to the mid 1980s with an increasing rate of warming after those dates. This was mentioned previously but is more visually apparent on thiss plot. As we shall see, this is the general trend of the temperature pattern for both the Northern Hemisphere and the Global temperatures series.



5 Inter Annual Temperature Variability

[1] "The Interannual Variability is: 0.755"


The “variability” is the noise around the signal. If the time series is not detrended, a steady warming trend will be incorrectly interpreted as high interannual variability. If a city warms by \(2^\circ\text{C}\) over 85 years perfectly smoothly, the standard deviation would be high, but the interannual variability (the “bounce” from one year to the next) would actually be zero. Using detrend() ensures you are measuring the year-to-year swings rather than the multi-decadal climate shift.

8 Change point detection - shifts in Ottawa’s Temperature

8.1 Is there a structural (regime) change in Ottawa’s historical temperature?

A strategy for long-term temperature data is to attempt to find true structural shifts (like climate regime shifts or even sensor changes). A nonparametric approach should be used which avoids assuming the temperature follows normal distribution (a bell shape curve), where many times the data often doesn’t.

Climate data is notoriously “noisy” due to seasonality (summer vs. winter) and local weather fluctuations. If you run a standard change point detection on the daily or monthly data, the algorithm will likely get “distracted” by the seasonal swings and identify a change point every six months. Therefore to examine the possibility of structural changes in the climate, we will look at the annual temperature series for Ottawa rather than other time perioderiods.

The statistical procedure for detecting structural changes is a change point algorithm developed by R. Killick and her colleagues (Ref and R package). The model used in this analysis employs a penalized likelihood approach to detect structural change-points in the temperature series which includes shifts in the mean, trend shifts and changes in the variance and uses the Bayesian Information Criteria (BIC) to indicate the optimal structural breakpoints.

What this plot tells us is that if the ribbon jumps up significantly, you’re seeing a clear “regime shift” where the new normal is entirely outside the old normal’s typical range.If the ribbon gets wider after a change point, it means the climate became more volatile (higher variance) in that segment, even if the average temperature didn’t change much.

Notice we are seeing a substantial jump in the temperature at around 1997 but statistically the breakpoint could occur anytime between 1990 and 2001 at the 2.5% level. However physically this is a striking change. Also notice the mean regime shift, when compared to the upward linear trend in temperature given by the dotted line on the graph, is at least 0.25 degrees greater.



A “Segmented Trend” model recognizes that the climate is a moving target. If the red lines are getting steeper with later segments, you have clear evidence of climate acceleration.


8.1.0.1 Interpreting “Acceleration”-look at the slope column in the table below:


Segment Start End Slope
1 1940 1997 0.0031

If segment 1 has the slope of \(0.0031\) and segment 2 has a slope of \(0.013\), the rate of warming has quintupled. The \(p\)-value for an segment 1 is high (e.g., \(> 0.05\)) but segment 2 is low (\(< 0.01\)), which indicates that warming has shifted from “random fluctuation” to a “statistically significant trend” in the later period.

In visualizing global vs. local trends, one really see the difference. It’s helpful to plot the individual segment slopes against a single trend line for the entire 85-year period.

10 Summary

This summary highlights the findings of the report titled “Ottawa’s 85 Year Temperature Report,” which examines local long temperature trends from 1940 to 2024 and compares them to global and Northern Hemisphere patterns[cite: 1].

10.0.1 Core Objectives

  • Purpose: The report investigates Ottawa’s alignment with global warming trends,
  • Timeframe: A continuous 85-year dataset spanning from 1940 to 2024[cite: 1].

10.0.2 Key Findings: Ottawa’s Warming Trend

  • Mean Temperature: The average temperature for the 85-year period is 6.3°C (\(+/- 11.2ºC\)) [cite: 1].
  • Acceleration: Significant warming began accelerating in the mid-1980s following a cooler period in the 1950s and 60s[cite: 1].
  • The “Winter Story”: Warming is most aggressive during winter months (DJF)[cite: 1]. The data shows that while Ottawa’s summers are getting hotter, our winters are warming at an even faster -roughly 3.3°C to 3.7°C since the late 1940s, compared to about 2.1°C for summers. December specifically shows a warming rate of 0.042°C per year, which is highly statistically significant (\(p < 0.001\))[cite: 1].
  • Amplification: Ottawa’s warming rate of +0.168°C/decade is roughly 27% faster than the global average (+0.133°C/decade)[cite: 1].

10.0.3 Structural Shifts & Regime Changes

  • Change Point Detection: A major “regime shift” or structural jump in temperature occurred around 1997[cite: 1].
  • Slope Quintupling: The warming rate shifted from a slope of 0.0031 (1940–1997) to 0.013 (1997–2024), effectively quintupling the rate of warming in the latter segment[cite: 1].
  • Extreme Events: The data confirms a transition from cold-extreme anomalies to heat-extreme anomalies, with a crossover point in the late 1980s[cite: 1].

10.0.4 Variability & Volatility

  • Interannual Variability (IAV): The report distinguishes between long-term climate shifts and year-to-year “noise”[cite: 1].
  • Volatility Peak: While the 2020s are warmer, the 1990s showed the highest climate instability with a volatility index of +/- 1.07°C[cite: 1].
  • The “Plateau”: Mid-century cooling (1940–1970) is noted as a result of post-WWII industrial aerosols[cite: 1].

10.0.5 Comparative Trends (1940–2024)

It is noticeable that Ottawa’s temperature trend is much steeper than the NH average, especially after 1980. This aligns with scientific findings that Canada is warming faster than either the NH orr global rate..

Ottawa’s data looks like a “heart monitor” (high volatility) compared to the smoother NH line. The reason for this is that NH averages smooths out local extremes by averaging oceans and continents together. Ottawa’s reality is that being in a continental interior, Ottawa is subject to massive swings—the loss of “extreme cold” years is actually one of the biggest drivers of the warming trend in Ottawa’s temperature data.

It is fascinating to see that the data confirm what many long-time residents suspect and that is, Ottawa climate is changing significantly due to the addition of greenhouse gases but alos, highlighting the continued influence of stochastic weather patterns and atmospheric teleconnections.
